content.text: Letters like P and Q stand for whole sentences. Parentheses show what each connective joins: 'both A and either B or C' is A ∧ (B ∨ C).
¬ applies to the smallest formula after it: ¬P ∨ Q denies only P, while ¬(P ∨ Q) denies the whole disjunction.

symbols.name: A → B
symbols.meaning: What follows 'only if' is the then part.

symbols.name: B → A
symbols.meaning: What follows 'if' is the if part.

symbols.name: A ↔ B
symbols.meaning: Each holds exactly when the other does.

examples.title: Not both
lines: You are not both rich and famous.
examples.note: The denial covers the whole conjunction.

examples.title: Neither
lines: You are neither rich nor famous.
examples.note: Neither A nor B denies the disjunction. That comes to not A and not B.

examples.title: A grouped conditional
lines: If you study, then you pass and you graduate.
examples.note: The and belongs inside the then part.

question.prompt: Which formula says 'If it rains, then the game is off or the field is covered'?
question.hint: Which part is the then part: the whole or sentence, or only its first half?
question.explanation: Everything after 'then' is the consequent, so the disjunction is grouped: R → (O ∨ C).
